packet.headline_seed: New science on algae die-offs is too late for the Reflecting Pool
packet.description_seed: Iron and hydrogen peroxide trigger cell death via ferroptosis, which cascades killer molecules through the population, causing mass die-offs of algae.

what: New science on algae die-offs is too late for the Reflecting Pool

clean_source_blocks.text: Iron and hydrogen peroxide trigger cell death via ferroptosis, which cascades killer molecules through the population, causing mass die-offs of algae.

The newly painted Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. was supposed to be “American Flag blue.” Instead, on June 16, the water turned an un-American shade of sickly green as an algal bloom burst through the water. While experts keep trying to eradicate the unsightly bloom, a research team has revealed new insights into how mass algal demise might happen naturally. A sudden algal die-off could be caused by an interaction between iron and hydrogen peroxide, researchers report June 25 in Science. The chemical reaction produces reactive molecules that burst cell membranes apart. Death could spread from a single cell to collapse an algal bloom if conditions are right. While the results could explain why at least some algal blooms die off, the findings can’t turn the Reflecting Pool blue. The situation there may be too far gone ---

Donald Trump has a new nemesis, with a name worthy of a supervillain: Scenedesmus. The Reflecting Pool on the National Mall has become the country’s most high-profile science experiment, with workers battling against nature. After a week of combat, they have essentially killed off one type of algae infesting the pool, only to create the conditions for a new type to take over. And Scenedesmus, a genus of green algae nicknamed “Skinny Dead Mouse” by scientists, is now flourishing, according to testing that was run at the request of The Atlantic.

Rosalina Stancheva Christova, a professor of aquatic ecology at George Mason University in Virginia, took water samples from the pool on Tuesday. She confirmed the algae belongs to the genus Desmodesmus, which she said is "growing in excessive amounts" but is not toxic or harmful. Christova says this kind of common green algae is found all over the region, especially this time of year. The reflecting pool in particular provides "excellent conditions" for algae growth, she said: shallow, stagnant water, strong sunlight and no shade. "It could happen every single summer," she added. "But it seems that the disturbance of the pond during the renovations [is] accelerating this process." Christova said last month's renovations may have affected the balance of nutrients in the pool, potentially accelerating the algae blooms. Goodale similarly views the resurfacing as one of several contributing factors.

WASHINGTON — The Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool is once again making headlines, this week for turning green.

The Washington, D.C. landmark was refilled with water earlier this month after President Trump had its neutral grey bottom repainted "American flag blue." The multimillion-dollar project produced subtle results in the eyes of many observers, even as Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum — whose agency managed the renovation — touted its success.

In recent days, however, the pool has taken on a verdant hue — the result of algae blooms that experts say are to be expected in these conditions.

payload.title: Uusi tutkimus selittää leväkukintojen äkkikuolemia, mutta ei pelasta Reflecting Poolia
payload.summary: Tuore tutkimus kuvaa mekanismin, jossa rauta ja vetyperoksidi voivat käynnistää leväsolujen kuoleman ja romahduttaa leväkukinnan. Washingtonin Reflecting Poolin vihertynyt vesi kertoo kuitenkin, että käytännön ongelma voi olla jo liian pitkällä.
payload.content:
Washingtonissa Lincoln Memorialin edustalla sijaitsevan Reflecting Poolin piti hohtaa uuden maalauksen jälkeen sinisenä, mutta kesäkuun puolivälissä vesi muuttui vihertäväksi leväkukinnan vuoksi. Samaan aikaan julkaistu tutkimus antaa uuden selityksen sille, miten levämassa voi luonnossa romahtaa nopeasti, mutta havainto ei tarjoa välitöntä ratkaisua altaan ongelmaan.

## Solukuolema voi levitä levämassassa

Tutkijoiden mukaan äkillinen leväkukinnan kuolema voi alkaa raudan ja vetyperoksidin vuorovaikutuksesta. Reaktio synnyttää erittäin reaktiivisia molekyylejä, jotka rikkovat solukalvoja. Prosessi liittyy ferroptoosiksi kutsuttuun solukuoleman muotoon.

Jos olosuhteet ovat sopivat, yhden solun kuolema voi käynnistää ketjureaktion. Tällöin vaurioittavat molekyylit leviävät leväpopulaatiossa ja voivat lopulta romahduttaa koko kukinnan. Tutkimus auttaa selittämään, miksi ainakin osa leväkukinnoista häviää luonnossa nopeasti.

Reflecting Poolin kohdalla tieto tulee kuitenkin myöhään. Allasta yritetään puhdistaa, mutta vihreä leväkasvu on jo päässyt näkyvästi valloilleen. Tutkimus ei siis tarkoita, että altaan vesi voitaisiin yksinkertaisesti palauttaa siniseksi samalla mekanismilla.

## Allas tarjoaa levälle hyvät olosuhteet

George Mason Universityn vesiekologian professori Rosalina Stancheva Christova otti altaasta vesinäytteitä ja arvioi, että levä kuuluu Desmodesmus-sukuun. Hänen mukaansa sitä kasvaa altaassa liiallisia määriä, mutta se ei ole myrkyllistä eikä haitallista.

Christovan mukaan tällainen vihreä levä on alueella tavallista etenkin tähän vuodenaikaan. Reflecting Pool on levälle erityisen suotuisa ympäristö, koska vesi on matalaa ja seisovaa, aurinko paistaa voimakkaasti eikä varjoa juuri ole.

Altaan hiljattainen kunnostus on voinut vauhdittaa kehitystä. Christovan mukaan remontti on saattanut muuttaa ravinteiden tasapainoa vedessä, mikä puolestaan voi kiihdyttää leväkukintoja. Myös muut asiantuntijat pitävät pinnoituksen uusimista yhtenä mahdollisena taustatekijänä.

Puhdistustyöt voivat lisäksi muuttaa altaan levälajistoa. Erään testauksen mukaan yhden levätyypin torjunta on voinut luoda tilaa toiselle vihreälle levälle. Tapaus näyttää, kuinka vaikeaa leväkukintaa on hallita, kun ympäristö tarjoaa sille jatkuvasti hyvät kasvuolosuhteet.
summary_bullets: Rauta ja vetyperoksidi voivat käynnistää leväsolujen kuolemaan johtavan reaktion.
Mekanismi voi sopivissa oloissa levitä solusta toiseen ja romahduttaa leväkukinnan.
Washingtonin Reflecting Poolin vihertymistä selittävät myös matala seisova vesi, voimakas aurinko ja mahdolliset kunnostuksen vaikutukset.
payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu annettuihin lähdekatkelmiin. Scenedesmus- ja Desmodesmus-havainnot käsiteltiin varovasti levälajiston muutoksina, koska lähteet nimeävät eri vihreän levän suvun.

Iron and hydrogen peroxide trigger cell death via ferroptosis, which cascades killer molecules through the population, causing mass die-offs of algae.

The newly painted Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. was supposed to be “American Flag blue.” Instead, on June 16, the water turned an un-American shade of sickly green as an algal bloom burst through the water. While experts keep trying to eradicate the unsightly bloom, a research team has revealed new insights into how mass algal demise might happen naturally. A sudden algal die-off could be caused by an interaction between iron and hydrogen peroxide, researchers report June 25 in Science. The chemical reaction produces reactive molecules that burst cell membranes apart. Death could spread from a single cell to collapse an algal bloom if conditions are right. While the results could explain why at least some algal blooms die off, the findings can’t turn the Reflecting Pool blue. The situation there may be too far gone ---

Donald Trump has a new nemesis, with a name worthy of a supervillain: Scenedesmus. The Reflecting Pool on the National Mall has become the country’s most high-profile science experiment, with workers battling against nature. After a week of combat, they have essentially killed off one type of algae infesting the pool, only to create the conditions for a new type to take over. And Scenedesmus, a genus of green algae nicknamed “Skinny Dead Mouse” by scientists, is now flourishing, according to testing that was run at the request of The Atlantic.

Rosalina Stancheva Christova, a professor of aquatic ecology at George Mason University in Virginia, took water samples from the pool on Tuesday. She confirmed the algae belongs to the genus Desmodesmus, which she said is "growing in excessive amounts" but is not toxic or harmful. Christova says this kind of common green algae is found all over the region, especially this time of year. The reflecting pool in particular provides "excellent conditions" for algae growth, she said: shallow, stagnant water, strong sunlight and no shade. "It could happen every single summer," she added. "But it seems that the disturbance of the pond during the renovations [is] accelerating this process." Christova said last month's renovations may have affected the balance of nutrients in the pool, potentially accelerating the algae blooms. Goodale similarly views the resurfacing as one of several contributing factors.
